prompt: Which clause does the database evaluate first?
hint: Nothing can be discarded before it is known what there is.

choices.why: Written first, evaluated near the end of the whole sequence.
It runs after the output columns have been computed.
It comes second, once the rows to filter are assembled.

choices.text: FROM, where the rows come from
choices.why: The rows have to exist before anything can be thrown away.

prompt: SELECT price * 1.23 AS gross … WHERE gross > 100 fails. Why?
hint: One of the two clauses had not run yet.

choices.why: It is, and that is where the alias came from.

choices.text: An alias may not be compared
choices.why: Aliases compare with anything their value compares with.
Quoting changes the case rule, not when the name exists.

choices.text: WHERE ran before the alias existed
choices.why: SELECT invents the name, and SELECT is later in the sequence.

prompt: The same alias works in ORDER BY. What does that tell you about the sequence?
hint: It is not a special case; it is a position.

choices.text: ORDER BY runs on the client side
choices.why: Sorting happens in the database like everything else.
They are created once, by SELECT.

choices.text: ORDER BY reads the table again
choices.why: It arranges what the query already produced.

choices.text: ORDER BY runs after the SELECT
choices.why: By the time it looks for the name, SELECT has created it.

prompt: Does rearranging the clauses of a query make it faster?
hint: Separate what a query means from what it costs.

choices.text: No, the evaluation order is fixed
choices.why: The order is logical; the planner does the work however it likes, and the answer is the same.

choices.text: Yes, when there is an ORDER BY
choices.why: Sorting is planned like everything else in the statement.

choices.text: Yes, clauses run in the written order
choices.why: They are not, and that is what the logical order is for.
The planner reorders conditions by its own estimates regardless of how you wrote them.

prompt: Put the clauses in the order the database evaluates them.
hint: The one you write first is not the one that runs first.
trap: The common swap is putting SELECT before WHERE, because that is the order they are written — and it is exactly the swap that makes the alias error look mysterious.

prompt: Where is SELECT * the right thing to write?
hint: One of these is a person looking, and the rest are programs.

choices.text: In a view, to follow the table
choices.why: A view's columns are fixed when it is created, which surprises people.

choices.text: At a terminal, exploring a table
choices.why: Everywhere else you get whatever the table happens to have today.

choices.text: In a report taking new columns
choices.why: That is the failure, not the feature: the report grows a column nobody asked for.
A schema change silently changes what the parser receives.

prompt: Which cost of SELECT * is the one lesson 9 will explain?
hint: One of them is about how the answer is found rather than what is sent.

choices.why: True, and it is about the network rather than the plan.
A query asking only for indexed columns can skip the table entirely.
True, and it is about the result rather than the cost.
True, and it is about the codebase rather than the database.

prompt: An expression in the SELECT list is given no alias. What is it called in the result?
hint: The database picks something, and it is not useful.

choices.why: Some clients show that; the column's actual name is not it.
Nothing borrows a name from an operand.

choices.text: An empty string the client fills
choices.why: The name is not empty; it is a placeholder.
Every client displays it and no program can rely on it.

prompt: The function that returns the first of its arguments that is not null, often used to give a missing value a display form: ___.
hint: One word, eight letters, and it is not a keyword.

prompt: WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-31' misses rows. Which?
hint: A bare date is a moment, and the moment is midnight.

choices.why: The upper bound is 2026-03-31 00:00:00, so the rest of that day is outside it.
Inclusive of a moment that is midnight, which is the trap.

choices.text: The whole of the 1st as well
choices.why: BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends, so the 1st is included.

choices.text: Rows that fall on a weekend
choices.why: Nothing about BETWEEN knows which day of the week a date is.

prompt: WHERE a = 'x' OR a = 'y' AND price < 50 — what did it mean?
hint: One of the two operators binds more tightly.

choices.text: Either x or y, both under 50
choices.why: That is the parenthesised version, and it is what was intended.
They are different queries returning different rows.

choices.text: x at any price, or y under 50
choices.why: AND binds tighter than OR, which is almost never what somebody writing this meant.
It parses perfectly, which is the problem.

prompt: Which of these can use an index on created_at?
hint: One of them leaves the column bare.

choices.why: The same problem again, and it also compares text.
The same problem in a different function.
The index knows the column's values, not the function's results.
A range of values the index is already sorted by.

prompt: The always-correct shape for a date range, in two operators: created_at ___ the start AND created_at ___ the start of the next period.
hint: The first is inclusive; the second is strict.

prompt: Which pattern can use an ordinary index?
hint: An index is sorted by the beginning of the value.

choices.why: The match can begin anywhere, so there is nothing to look up.
A regular expression, and not indexable in the general case.
Same problem, and the case folding on top of it.
Values that start alike sort together, so it is a range lookup.

prompt: A search box passes what the user typed straight into a LIKE pattern. What goes wrong?
hint: Two of the characters they might type are not ordinary characters.

choices.why: LIKE was always case sensitive; that is not caused by the input.
A % matches everything and nobody can reproduce the report.

choices.text: A quote in the input is refused
choices.why: A quote is a quoting problem and a different one.

choices.text: The pattern stops at the first space
choices.why: Spaces are ordinary characters in a pattern.

prompt: Where does a format rule such as a SKU shape really belong?
hint: Ask whether you would rather refuse it or filter it.

choices.text: In the application, before the insert
choices.why: Which holds until the import script, as lesson 1 argued.

choices.text: In a CHECK constraint on the table
choices.why: Checking once at write time is cheaper and stronger than filtering at read time.

choices.text: In a trigger that rewrites them
choices.why: Rewriting somebody's data silently is worse than refusing it.

choices.text: In a regex, repeated per query
choices.why: Which has to be remembered by everyone who writes a query.

prompt: Ten products, three with no category. = 'kitchen' gives 4 and <> 'kitchen' gives 3. Where are the rest?
hint: WHERE keeps a row when the condition is true.

choices.text: In the second; they are not kitchen
choices.why: Nobody knows what they are, so the condition is unknown rather than true.
They are counted zero times, not twice.

choices.text: Excluded by the database as invalid
choices.why: They are valid rows with one unknown column.

choices.text: In neither of the two results
choices.why: Unknown is not true, so the row fails both conditions.

prompt: WHERE NOT (price > 100). What happens to a row whose price is unknown?
hint: NOT of unknown is still unknown.

choices.text: It is kept; unknown is not over 100
choices.why: That reasoning is a person's; the database says unknown.

choices.text: The query is refused as invalid
choices.why: It is valid SQL and returns an answer.

choices.text: It is dropped from the result
choices.why: Negating a condition gives the rows where it was definitely false, not the ones it excluded.

choices.text: It is kept; NOT flips the failure
choices.why: NOT unknown is unknown, and unknown is not true.

prompt: A subquery inside NOT IN returns one NULL among its values. What comes back?
hint: Unfold the NOT IN into a chain of ANDs.

choices.why: No error is raised, which is what makes it dangerous.

choices.text: Every row, since NULL matches nothing
choices.why: It matches nothing and poisons the chain instead.

choices.text: No rows at all, whatever the data
choices.why: The unknown term makes the whole AND unable to be true, and nothing is reported.

choices.text: The rows outside the non-null values
choices.why: That is what people expect and not what happens.

prompt: Which operator answers true or false even when one side is null?
hint: It treats null as a value that is simply different.

choices.why: Ordinary <> says unknown; this one commits to an answer.
That works and it also hides the index, which is a separate cost.
Bracketing an unknown is still unknown.
A condition on the list, and it does not help the column being null.

prompt: In the three-valued logic, what is false AND unknown?
hint: One operand already settles the question.

choices.why: The unknown does not always spread; here the answer is known either way.
Nothing here could make it true.
It is one of the three truth values.
It would be, if the other operand left the question open.

prompt: = NULL is valid SQL that is never true. The two operators that ask about the state instead are IS NULL and IS ___ NULL.
hint: One short word.

prompt: A query has no ORDER BY. What order do the rows come back in?
hint: A table is a set.

choices.why: And it changes when the table grows, an index appears or the planner picks another route.
Common on a small table, which is what makes the habit dangerous.
Only if the plan happens to read that index, which is not promised.
Nothing remembers the previous run.

prompt: ORDER BY a, b DESC. Which direction is a sorted in?
hint: Each key carries its own direction.

choices.why: It applies to the key it follows.

choices.text: Descending for a, ascending for b
choices.why: That is the reverse of what was written.
DESC applies to b alone, which catches people who expect it to cover both.
Nothing about a sort direction is left to the planner.

prompt: ORDER BY category LIMIT 10, with twenty rows in that category. Which ten come back?
hint: The sort says nothing about ties.

choices.text: The ten that were inserted first
choices.why: Insertion order is not recorded anywhere.

choices.text: It is undefined, and varies by run
choices.why: Which is why the sort has to end on something unique.
Nothing randomises; it is simply not settled.

choices.text: The ten with the lowest primary key
choices.why: Only by accident of the plan, and not by promise.

prompt: Where do nulls sort in PostgreSQL, ascending?
hint: It treats them as larger than everything.

choices.why: That is MySQL's choice, which is why the difference matters.
The order is defined by the language, not the index.
And first descending — and MySQL chooses the opposite, so say NULLS LAST.
Sorting never drops rows.

prompt: ORDER BY (price > 100) DESC, name. What does that produce?
hint: A boolean sorts false before true.

choices.why: DESC reverses that, which is why it is there.
Nothing is filtered; an ORDER BY does not discard.

choices.text: An error, since a boolean sorts badly
choices.why: Booleans sort like any other type.

choices.text: The dear ones first, then by name
choices.why: Which is how you say these first, then everything else, in one query.

prompt: What does OFFSET 100000 actually do?
hint: There is no way to know which row is the hundred-thousandth without producing the ones before it.

choices.text: Reads backwards from the end of the index
choices.why: It has no notion of how far from the end it is.
Which is why page 1 is instant and page 5,000 times out.
Nothing records a row's position in an order.

choices.text: Asks the planner where to start
choices.why: There is no such starting point to ask for.

prompt: Somebody reads page 1 and a row is inserted that sorts above everything. They click page 2. What do they see?
hint: Everything below the insert shifted by one.

choices.text: The new row at the top of their page 2
choices.why: It sorts above everything, so it is on page 1 now.

choices.text: An error, because the result changed under them
choices.why: Nothing detects that.

choices.text: Page 2 as it would have been before the insert
choices.why: The offset counts from the current state, not from when they loaded page 1.

choices.text: A row they already saw, and one they never will
choices.why: No error, nothing in a log, and it depends on somebody else's timing.

prompt: Why does keyset pagination cost the same on page 20,000 as on page 2?
hint: It never counts anything.

choices.why: Nothing is cached between statements.

choices.text: It jumps in and walks twenty entries
choices.why: The cursor is a value, not a position, so there is nothing to skip.
Direction is not what makes it cheap.
Each page is its own statement over the index.

prompt: What does keyset pagination give up?
hint: One thing people object to, and it is worth asking what it costs.

choices.why: A page is defined by where the last one ended rather than by a count.

choices.text: Using an index for the sort
choices.why: It depends on one more than offset paging does.

choices.text: Working on a table being written
choices.why: That is the case it is built for.
It goes both ways; the comparison is simply reversed.

prompt: Comparing several sort keys at once, standard SQL lets you compare the whole ___: (created_at, id) < ('…', 4711).
hint: One word for a fixed-length group of values compared left to right.

prompt: SELECT DISTINCT category, name FROM products removes almost nothing. Why?
hint: It applies to something wider than one column.

choices.text: The rows differ in unselected columns
choices.why: Only the selected columns are compared.

choices.text: It deduplicates the pair of columns
choices.why: Distinct pairs, and name is nearly unique, so almost every pair is.
It considers all of them together.

choices.text: DISTINCT is ignored with two columns
choices.why: It is applied, to the combination.

prompt: SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON … — what does the DISTINCT hide?
hint: Ask where the duplicates came from.

choices.why: Possible, and then DISTINCT is wrong rather than wasteful.
The rows are distinct; the join repeats the customer.

choices.text: No defect; it is the standard spelling
choices.why: EXISTS is, and it creates no duplication to remove.

prompt: DISTINCT ON (customer_id) … ORDER BY customer_id, ordered_on DESC. Which row survives per customer?

choices.text: The one with the lowest id

choices.text: Each of them, in an array

prompt: UNION against UNION ALL — which is the expensive one?
hint: One of them has to compare rows with each other.

choices.text: It depends on the indexes there
choices.why: Indexes help each side; the deduplication happens after.

prompt: You add a condition and the count does not change. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The table is too small to tell
